lead: The weekday readings speak about wealth. James warns the rich who have kept back the wages of their workers: their riches are rotting, and the cry of the labourers has reached the Lord of hosts. In Luke, Jesus says it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God, and when the disciples ask who then can be saved, he answers that what is impossible for people is possible for God. Today the Church also remembers Saints Joachim and Anne, the parents of the Virgin Mary according to tradition, and offers readings for them about God who gives life to the barren: Hannah’s song, Isaiah’s “Sing, O barren one”, Abraham and Sarah in the Letter to the Hebrews, and the genealogy of Jesus in Matthew. The two sets meet in one truth: what people cannot do, God can, and he lifts up the poor and the lowly.

set: The Letter of James is addressed to Jewish Christians “in the Dispersion” (1:1). Its writer is James, whom tradition identifies with the “brother of the Lord”, the leader of the Church in Jerusalem; some scholars think it was written in his name a little later. The letter is full of concern for the poor. Here, in the manner of the prophets, James turns to the rich landowners and speaks of judgment. He is not condemning wealth in itself but wealth gained by fraud and kept at the cost of others.
str: vv. 1–3: the rich must weep and wail; their riches rot, their gold rusts, and the rust will bear witness against them.
v. 4: the wages kept back by fraud cry out; the cry of the harvesters has reached the Lord of hosts.
vv. 5–6: lives of luxury; hearts fattened for a day of slaughter; the righteous one condemned and killed.
kw: The word of the prophets for the cry of anguish at coming judgment (for example Isaiah 13:6). James speaks like Amos and Isaiah.
The pay of labourers. The Law commanded that a hired worker be paid on the same day (Leviticus 19:13; Deuteronomy 24:14–15), because he is poor and depends on it.
Used in the New Testament only here and in Romans 9:29. It recalls the Lord who commands heaven’s armies and takes the side of the oppressed.
vv: Your riches have rotted, and your clothes are moth-eaten.
In the ancient world wealth was stored as grain, garments and metal. James says these treasures are already perishing, and what is hoarded is lost.
Listen! The wages of the laborers who mowed your fields, which you kept back by fraud, cry out
The wages themselves cry out, as Abel’s blood cried from the ground (Genesis 4:10). God hears what no judge heard.
You have condemned and murdered the righteous one, who does not resist you.
It may mean the poor and innocent, who cannot defend themselves in court. Christians have also heard in it an echo of the Righteous One, Christ (Acts 3:14; 7:52).
ch: The Catechism teaches that a just wage is the legitimate fruit of work, and that to refuse or withhold it can be a grave injustice (CCC 2434, citing this letter and Leviticus 19:13, Deuteronomy 24:14–15, James 5:4). It lists the injustice done to wage earners among the sins that cry to heaven (CCC 1867). Passages such as this one are among the roots of the Church’s social teaching on the dignity of work.

r.h: What is impossible for mortals is possible for God
set: The passage follows the story of a rich ruler who asked what he must do to inherit eternal life and went away sad when Jesus asked him to sell his possessions and give to the poor (18:18–24). Jesus looks at him and says how hard it is for the wealthy to enter the kingdom. The camel and the needle’s eye is a deliberate exaggeration, a picture of what is humanly impossible. The idea that “the Needle’s Eye” was a low gate in Jerusalem is a later story with no support in the ancient texts.
str: v. 25: a camel through the eye of a needle is easier than a rich person entering the kingdom.
vv. 26–27: “Then who can be saved?” “What is impossible for mortals is possible for God.”
vv. 28–30: Peter: “Look, we have left our homes and followed you.” Jesus promises much more in this age and eternal life in the age to come.
kw: The answer turns on these two words. Salvation is not earned by human strength, whether rich or poor, but given by God’s power.
The question of the crowd is the question of every hearer. For Luke, salvation is already present in Jesus, and the poor and sinners are among the first to receive it.
Luke’s word for what is received in return. Mark has “a hundredfold” and adds “with persecutions” (10:30). What the disciple receives is not riches but a larger family, the community of believers.
vv: it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for someone who is rich to enter the kingdom of God.
The danger is not money as such but the heart that clings to it. Riches can fill the heart so that there is no room for God and neighbour.
What is impossible for mortals is possible for God.
This is the Gospel in one line. The rich person can be saved, as can the poor, because grace can open what human effort cannot.

there is no one who has left house or wife or brothers or parents or children, for the sake of the kingdom of God, who will not get back very much more in this age, and in the age to come eternal life.
The reward is promised both now and then. Those who give up their own security for the Gospel find a family of faith and the joy of belonging to Christ.
ch: St Clement of Alexandria wrote a whole treatise on this passage, Who Is the Rich Man That Is Saved? He taught in substance that what Jesus asks us to renounce is the passion for riches, not the possession of goods, and that a rich person can be saved by using wealth to help others. The Catechism teaches that poverty of heart is a requirement of the Gospel: the Lord asks his disciples to prefer him to everything and everyone (CCC 2544–2547), while those called to the evangelical counsels give up everything to follow him (CCC 915–916). It also teaches love for the poor as the sign of authentic discipleship (CCC 2443–2446).

set: Hannah, wife of Elkanah, was barren and prayed at the sanctuary of Shiloh for a child. God gave her Samuel, and she brought him to serve the Lord (1:1–2:11). This song is her thanksgiving. Its themes are the reversal of fortunes: the strong are broken, the weak are raised, the poor are seated with princes. The name Anne is the Greek form of Hannah, which means “favour, grace”.
str: vv. 1–2: joy in the Lord, the Holy One and Rock.
vv. 3–8: the proud are brought down; the barren bears seven; the Lord raises the poor from the dust.
vv. 9–10: the Lord guards the faithful; the Lord judges the ends of the earth and exalts his anointed.
kw: A name for God as the unshakable refuge of his people (compare Deuteronomy 32:4).
The last word of the song. In its first sense it is the king of Israel; the Church also hears the Messiah, whom Mary’s own song, the Magnificat, will recall.
vv: The bows of the mighty are broken, but the feeble gird on strength.
God’s way overturns human strength. The weak are not helpless because the Lord is their strength.
He raises up the poor from the dust; he lifts the needy from the ash heap
This is the verse behind many psalms and the Magnificat: Mary says he has “lifted up the lowly” (Luke 1:52).
ch: The Church has always seen Hannah’s prayer as the model for Mary’s Magnificat (Luke 1:46–55); the two songs share the same movement of praise for a God who raises the lowly (CCC 2619). Today Saint Anne, who tradition says was granted a child after long waiting, is honoured as a woman of the same faith.

set: These verses come from the second part of Isaiah, addressed to the exiles in Babylon in the sixth century before Christ. Jerusalem, left desolate, is pictured as a barren woman and a forsaken wife. God now calls her to sing and to enlarge her tent, for her children will be more than ever. The “Maker” who is her husband has not abandoned her for good.
str: vv. 1–3: sing, enlarge your tent; your descendants will fill the nations.
vv. 4–6: do not fear; your Maker is your husband; the Lord calls you back like a wife forsaken.
vv. 7–8: for a brief moment I abandoned you; with everlasting love I will have compassion on you.
kw: The close relative who rescues a family member from slavery or debt (Ruth 4). God takes on that role for his people.
Raḥămîm comes from the word for womb: the mother’s tenderness. The same Lord who seems silent for a moment loves with a love that does not end.
vv: Enlarge the site of your tent, and let the curtains of your habitations be stretched out
Faith prepares room before the gift arrives. Hope enlarges the heart.
For a brief moment I abandoned you, but with great compassion I will gather you.
The shadows are real but brief. God’s final word is not abandonment but the gathering of his people.
ch: The Church applies verse 1 to the barren who become mothers by God’s grace: Sarah, Hannah, Elizabeth, and Saint Anne. Saint Paul applies the same verse to the Jerusalem above, our mother (Galatians 4:26–27). The Catechism teaches that God’s power is shown in the weakness and lowly estate of those he chooses (CCC 64, 489, on the holy women of the Old Testament who prepared for Mary).

set: The Letter to the Hebrews, written to Jewish Christians who were tempted to lose heart, presents a long list of people of faith in chapter 11. Abraham and Sarah stand at the head: they trusted the promise of a land and a child when both seemed impossible. The reading is chosen for Joachim and Anne because they too, according to tradition, waited long for a child.
str: vv. 8–10: Abraham obeys the call, lives in tents as a stranger, and looks for the city whose builder is God.
vv. 11–12: by faith Abraham, too old and with Sarah barren, received power of procreation; from one man, as good as dead, came descendants like the stars.
kw: In Hebrews, faith is trust that holds fast to what is promised though it is not yet seen (11:1).
The two words for the maker of the city. Abraham looks for a city that human hands did not found.
vv: By faith Abraham obeyed when he was called to set out for a place that he was to receive as an inheritance; and he set out, not knowing where he was going.
Faith moves before the road is clear. Abraham is the pattern of obedient trust.
because he considered him faithful who had promised.
The reason for hope is not our strength but the faithfulness of God who promises.
ch: The Catechism points to Abraham as the model of faith in his obedience to the call (CCC 144–147) and to Sarah, whose child Isaac was born by God’s promise (CCC 706). The Church holds up these ancestors in faith to the families who wait on God. Saints Joachim and Anne are remembered in the Church as a couple of the same patient trust.

r.h: The genealogy of Jesus the Messiah
set: Matthew opens his Gospel with the family tree of Jesus, arranged in three sets of fourteen generations (v. 17), from Abraham to David, from David to the exile in Babylon, and from the exile to the Messiah. In Hebrew letters the name David adds up to fourteen, a clue to the pattern. Jesus is presented as son of Abraham, the father of the people, and son of David, the king.

Unusually for a Jewish genealogy, four women are named: Tamar, Rahab, Ruth and “the wife of Uriah” (Bathsheba). The list ends with a break in the pattern: Joseph is “the husband of Mary, of whom Jesus was born”. It is Mary, not Joseph, through whom Jesus is born, and Matthew goes on to tell of his conception by the Holy Spirit (1:18–25). The names of Joachim and Anne do not appear in Scripture; they come from the second-century Protoevangelium of James, an early writing the Church does not receive as Scripture, and tradition has kept the names.
str: v. 1: the title: the genealogy of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham.
vv. 2–6: from Abraham to David, including Tamar, Rahab and Ruth.
vv. 7–11: from Solomon to the exile in Babylon.
vv. 12–16: from the exile to Joseph, the husband of Mary, of whom Jesus was born.
kw: The same words as the opening of Genesis in the Greek Bible (Genesis 2:4; 5:1). Matthew begins a new genesis, a new creation, in Christ.
The Greek for “anointed”. The first verse names Jesus as the Messiah, son of David.
vv: An account of the genealogy of Jesus the Messiah, the son of David, the son of Abraham.
In one line, Matthew places Jesus in the whole story of Israel. The promise to Abraham and the promise to David meet in him.
and Jacob the father of Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom Jesus was born, who is called the Messiah.
The pattern “father of” breaks here. Joseph is not named as Jesus’ father but as Mary’s husband: Jesus is born of Mary.
ch: The Church reads the genealogy as proof that God’s promises are kept through history, including through sinners and foreigners. The Catechism teaches that Mary, the daughter of Zion, is the one in whom the long preparation of the Old Covenant reaches its goal (CCC 489). The Church honours the parents of the Virgin Mary in this tradition of those who handed on faith, and Mary’s own descent from David has been the common teaching of Christians from early times.

qa: Who were Saints Joachim and Anne?

The Gospels do not name the parents of the Virgin Mary. The names Joachim and Anne come from the Protoevangelium of James, written in the second century. The Church does not treat this book as Scripture or as a reliable historical source for its details, but the names have been honoured in the East from early centuries and in the West from the Middle Ages, and 26 July is kept for them. They are remembered as the grandparents of Jesus according to tradition, and as an example of faithful parents who handed on the faith.
Does the Gospel say the rich cannot be saved?

No. Jesus says it is hard, not that it is impossible, and he says that all things are possible for God. Zacchaeus, a rich man, was saved when he gave half his goods to the poor and repaid those he had cheated (Luke 19:1–10). The danger is the heart that clings to riches and forgets God and neighbour.
rite: Saints Joachim and Anne remind the Syro-Malabar family of the part grandparents play in handing on the faith. In many Kerala homes it is the grandmother who teaches the first prayers and the grandfather who leads the evening prayer, and these are among the things the parish and the eparchy are glad to protect. The readings of the day also ask how a family uses its goods: the wages owed to workers, the generosity of the home, and the trust in God’s power that is greater than our plans.
study: James says the wages held back “cry out” to the Lord. Do I pay a fair wage and a fair price, and do I listen to the workers whose labour I use?
Jesus says that what is impossible for people is possible for God. What do I think is impossible in my life, and can I place it in his hands?
Hannah, Sarah and Anne waited long for a child. What am I waiting for, and how do I wait in faith?
